summaries.example: Imagine two choices: one helps many people enjoy friendship and beautiful music, while the other causes a lot of pain. Moore’s view says we should usually choose the choice that creates the most overall good, counting everyone’s good equally. He also says a good result can be more valuable when its parts fit together in a special way.
summaries.summary: G.E. Moore argued that goodness is objective: moral claims can be true or false even when people disagree. He called this moral realism. He also said goodness is not the same thing as a scientific fact, pleasure, desire, or anything else studied in a non-moral way. His famous open-question argument asks us to notice that even after learning that something is pleasant, we can still ask, “But is it good?” Moore thought this shows that “good” has its own meaning. In practical ethics, he defended a form of consequentialism: the right choice is the one that produces the most total good for everyone, considered fairly. He thought the best things included appreciation of beauty and personal love, though he treated these ideas in a distinctive and sometimes limited way. He also said that a whole can have value that is not just the value of its pieces added together. Philosophers have criticized and defended parts of his theory, and his arguments remain important in discussions about value and moral truth.
key_ideas: Moore thought goodness is a real feature, not merely a name for what someone likes.
He said asking whether pleasure is good remains a meaningful question, so goodness is not simply the same as pleasure.
He believed we should count everyone’s good fairly, rather than giving only our own good importance.
He especially valued loving relationships and enjoying beauty, though his views about which things are good changed in some details.
His ideas were debated, but they continued to influence later moral philosophy.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore gives us tools for asking what makes something valuable. His ideas help separate questions about facts, feelings, and goodness. They also invite us to think about fairness: should our choices help only ourselves, or should they consider everyone? Even people who reject Moore’s conclusions often discuss his questions about whether goodness can be reduced to pleasure, desire, or science.

important_terms.definition: The view that some moral truths are real and do not depend only on what people believe or feel.
Moore’s idea that goodness cannot be fully explained by science, pleasure, desire, or another non-moral fact.
A test that asks whether something can still be questioned as good even after we learn that it is pleasant or desired.
The view that the right action is the one that creates the greatest total good for everyone.
The idea that a whole can have more or less value than simply adding the values of its separate parts.

questions_to_think_about: Is something good because people enjoy it, or can it be good for another reason?
Should we count everyone’s happiness equally when making a choice?
Can a team, friendship, or piece of music be better than the separate parts considered alone?

summaries.example: Suppose a policy produces the greatest amount of pleasure but also destroys people’s opportunities to appreciate truth, beauty, or one another. A simple hedonist may judge the policy by pleasure alone. Moore’s ideal consequentialism asks about a wider range of intrinsic goods and says the correct policy is the one with the greatest impartial total value. It also allows that following general rules may produce better results than calculating every individual act.
summaries.summary:
G.E. Moore’s moral philosophy has two connected sides. In metaethics, he defended non-naturalist moral realism: moral judgments are objectively true or false, but ethical truth is not reducible to scientific, psychological, or other non-moral truth. He treated goodness as a simple, unanalyzable concept and appealed to the open-question argument. If “good” meant “pleasant,” then asking whether pleasure is good would be equivalent to asking whether pleasure is pleasant; yet the former appears substantive and disputable. Critics argue that this may establish only a difference between concepts, not between properties, and the entry emphasizes that no consensus has settled the argument. Moore also held that basic moral knowledge involves intuition, understood as direct recognition rather than inference, while acknowledging that intuitive judgments can be mistaken.

In normative ethics, Moore defended impersonal consequentialism: right action maximizes total good without giving one person’s good greater basic weight. His account was perfectionist or ideal rather than purely hedonist. He identified aesthetic appreciation and personal love as major goods, treated pain as a very serious evil, and allowed several ultimate values. His principle of organic unities says that the value of a complex whole need not equal the sum of the independent values of its parts. Moore’s views changed in some respects between Principia Ethica and Ethics, and his account of love has been criticized as too contemplative and insufficiently attentive to attachment, action, happiness, and achievement. The entry presents his influence as substantial but contested: his ideas helped shape later debates among realism, non-cognitivism, naturalism, consequentialism, and other ethical theories.
key_ideas: Moore’s non-naturalist realism combines objective moral truth with the autonomy of ethics; it is not merely the view that moral language reports attitudes.

The open-question argument targets reductions of goodness to pleasure, desire, evolutionary success, or other natural properties, though critics dispute whether it establishes a metaphysical difference between properties.
Moore treated good as the fundamental normative concept in Principia Ethica, while later work gave “ought” a more independent status.
His ideal consequentialism values states such as aesthetic appreciation and personal love, not only pleasure or desire satisfaction.
His impartialism rejects restricting moral concern to one’s own good, although the entry notes tensions in his treatment of egoism and “good for.”
Moore’s influence extended beyond his own theory: later philosophers adopted, criticized, or revised his realism, intuitionism, consequentialism, and account of value.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore’s philosophy clarifies several questions that remain central to ethics: whether moral truths are objective, whether value can be reduced to natural facts, how we know moral principles, and whether consequences should determine right action. His work also shows how a theory can combine impartial moral concern with a rich account of goods such as beauty and love. Studying the objections to his arguments is important because the disputes concern the very methods philosophy should use when reasoning about value.

important_terms.definition: The metaethical claim that moral or normative judgments can be objectively true or false, independently of anyone’s attitudes.
The claim that ethical concepts and truths are not reducible to non-moral scientific or metaphysical concepts.
Moore’s argument that identifying goodness with a natural property does not settle whether that property is good; the question remains substantively open.
The view that “good” is a basic concept or property that cannot be analyzed into simpler non-moral terms.
The normative theory that right action maximizes total good, impartially counting each person’s good.
The claim that several kinds of things may be intrinsically valuable, rather than there being only one ultimate good such as pleasure.
Moore’s claim that a whole may have value beyond, or below, the values its parts would have separately.
Knowledge of basic moral truths through direct recognition rather than inference from non-moral premises; Moore did not treat it as infallible.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that “pleasure is good” remains debatable show that goodness is not identical to pleasure, or only that concepts can differ from properties?
Can a theory maximize value while also recognizing special obligations to friends and family?
If a whole has organic value, where should that additional value be located: in the whole itself or in its parts?
What would a fallible form of moral intuition need in order to be reliable?
Does Moore’s account of personal love leave enough room for loyalty to particular people?

summaries.example: A school must choose between two plans. Plan A gives students more exciting entertainment for a week. Plan B creates a lasting music program, strengthens friendships, and prevents serious harm, although it is less immediately fun. Moore would ask which plan produces the most total good for everyone. He might also say that the value of the program is not just the separate value of music and friendship: together, they may form a more valuable whole.
summaries.summary:
G.E. Moore developed a theory about both the meaning of moral ideas and the best way to act. He defended moral realism, the idea that moral statements can be objectively true or false. He also argued for non-naturalism: goodness is not identical to pleasure, desire, popularity, scientific facts, or some other non-moral property. His open-question argument illustrates this. Even after someone says, “This is pleasant,” it still makes sense to ask, “Yes, but is it good?” Moore believed that this question is not settled just by understanding the word or by learning a natural fact. Some philosophers think this argument succeeds; others say it confuses differences between concepts with differences between properties.

Moore’s practical theory is a form of ideal consequentialism. It says that right actions produce the greatest total good, with everyone’s good counted impartially. However, Moore did not think pleasure was the only good. He emphasized aesthetic appreciation and personal love, and he defended value pluralism, the view that there can be several basic kinds of value. His principle of organic unities says that a whole may be better or worse than the simple sum of its parts. He also described moral knowledge as intuitive, meaning that some moral truths are recognized directly rather than inferred from science, while allowing that people can make mistakes. Moore’s work became highly influential, even though later philosophers challenged his arguments, his specific list of goods, and his strongly impartial account of love and value.
key_ideas: Moore separated moral truth from personal approval and from scientific descriptions of the world.
He argued that “good” cannot simply mean “pleasant,” “wanted,” or “highly evolved,” because we can still question whether those things are good.
He thought “good” was the basic moral idea, although his later writings treated “ought” as a distinct concept.
Moore’s theory of right action looks at total results and gives equal basic importance to each person.
He defended more than one kind of ultimate value, especially aesthetic appreciation and personal love.
His arguments attracted strong criticism, but they influenced many later debates about moral language and value.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moore helps us distinguish three questions: what people feel, what facts science describes, and what is genuinely good or right. That distinction can improve everyday reasoning about choices and public decisions. His theory also makes fairness a central issue while refusing to reduce all value to pleasure. Whether one agrees with him or not, his arguments provide a clear starting point for examining how moral judgments work and what reasons we have to act.

important_terms.definition: The view that moral claims can be true or false independently of what individuals or groups happen to think.
Moore’s claim that moral ideas cannot be reduced to ordinary scientific or psychological facts.
Moore’s question-based argument: even if something is pleasant or desired, we can still sensibly ask whether it is good.
The view that an action is right when its results contain the greatest total amount of good.
The idea that there can be several basic kinds of value, such as beauty and loving relationships.
The idea that a combination of parts can have a value different from simply adding the parts’ separate values.
A way of knowing a basic moral truth directly rather than proving it from other kinds of facts.
The position that everyone’s good should count equally in moral decision-making.

questions_to_think_about: If everyone in a group approves of something, does that make it good? Why or why not?
Could pleasure be valuable without being the only valuable thing?
Is it fair to sacrifice one person’s benefit to create much greater benefits for many others?
When friends work together, can their shared achievement be worth more than the separate efforts?
Should moral intuitions be trusted if thoughtful people disagree about them?
